transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: Endless Rain [H-01], The Causeway Wardens [F-03].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the plank roofs of Hollowmoot as you file toward the toll-gate at the market end of the stilt-town, where the Causeway Wardens have strung chains across the walkway and a queue of soaked refugees waits under guttering lanterns. Torches hiss against the downpour; a Warden sergeant with red-rimmed eyes checks names against a waterlogged ledger while two more stand the chain with hooks and burn-brands, watching every cough in the crowd like it might be the hive. Somewhere behind you the market stalls sell charms and dried fish under tarps, and somewhere ahead, past the chain, is whatever brought each of you to this crossing tonight. The Wardens are undermanned and frightened, and it shows — short tempers, quick chains, a fire already lit and waiting.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I know you, Rell. I know what you're really looking for.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps out of the crowd and approaches Warden Sergeant Rell, her eyes carefully studying his patterns—which refugees he scrutinizes closely, which ones pass easily, where his fear truly lies beneath the official procedures. She watches the hooks, the fire, the way his fingers grip his ledger.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Sergeant, I'm trained in the old exorcism rites. I know the marks the hive leaves that others miss—I can help you sift the truly sick from those just soaked and scared.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward from the crowd, moving with the quiet confidence of someone who has actually faced the thing that keeps these Wardens awake at night. He approaches Sergeant Rell directly, keeping his hands visible and his voice low and steady against the rain.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Sergeant. I'm Caddock, the midwife. I've got work waiting on the other side of that chain, and neither of us has time for bureaucracy.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock strides through the queue toward Sergeant Rell, water streaming off her heavy cloak, moving with the unshakeable confidence of someone who has made life-or-death decisions in far worse weather. She doesn't wait her turn—she walks straight to the chain.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Sergeant Rell—you're stretched thin and scared, and that's when mistakes happen. Let Brack do what he was born for. He'll know the hive-touched before they ever cough.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow pushes through the crowd toward the chain with Brack at his heel, movements deliberate and calm. He lets the hound range along the edge of the refugee queue—even in the downpour, Brack's scarred muzzle works methodically at the air, inhaling deep, tracking infection through flood and rain like he's done a hundred times before in the Sallowmere. Meanwhile, Yarrow's own eyes move across the waiting people, reading the subtle signs: tremor in the hands, that peculiar glassy stare, the way fever makes a person hunch. His experience shows.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — create advantage with Notice: dice + - + + → Fantastic (+6) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — create advantage with Lore: dice - - - -, invoking Knows the old exorcism rites of Saint Orrin [AN-03], Trained to purge the hive from flesh himself [AN-04], Reads the ruined liturgy others can't [AN-03] → Fantastic (+6) vs Good (+3): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Notice: dice 0 0 - -, invoking Brack tracks scent through any flood [YA-02] → Great (+4) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rell's ledger stops moving. Petra watches him flinch at the word 'looking'—she's read him true: he isn't hunting the hive-touched at all, he's terrified of what happens when Hollowmoot finds out how few chains they really have. Anselm's steady recitation of the old marks, spoken low and sure, settles something in the sergeant's shoulders; here, finally, is someone who won't waste his time guessing. Brack noses down the queue and comes up clean, tail low but certain, and Yarrow reads the same in the crowd's trembling hands — no sickness here, only cold and fear, and Rell's men ease their grips on the hooks. Caddock doesn't even have to raise her voice; she simply walks through the gap the others have opened, and Rell waves her past with the distracted nod of a man who has decided, in the space of one conversation, that these four aren't his problem tonight. The chain drops. Behind you Hollowmoot's lantern-lit market sprawls into the dark, tarps sagging under the endless rain, and whatever business brought each of you here is, at last, within reach.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Vess, I remember those days at the toll-gate—you're right, I still owe you for that crossing. I'm good for it when things settle, but right now I need to know: what's the favor?

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts the compel on 'A Stranded Ferryman'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Vess doesn't lead you to Rell's lean-to after all — he glances at the sergeant's chained gate, then jerks his chin toward the black water lapping under the pilings. Down a rickety ladder, his punt sits half-swamped at its mooring, and he's bailing it with a dented pot, cursing under his breath. "Not here," he mutters, eyes flicking to the shadows between the stilts. "Owe the Wardens for the mooring fee, owe the Marrows for the pole, owe half the ferry-row for favors I can't remember taking. You want passage past the chains quiet-like? Help me get this boat seaworthy and gone before sunup, and I'll owe you instead of them." Rain drums on the punt's cracked hull, each new leak a reminder of just how many debts are catching up to him at once.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Vess, the west pilings—see how the water runs faster there, how it pulls? That's your channel past their chains. Rain like this drowns the sound, and they won't see us slip through.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra kicks off her boots and peers into the black water churning around the stilts, her eyes tracing how the pilings slice through the current. The rain drums its endless rhythm, and in that sound—that press of water against wood—she feels something her fingers learned at the ferry-work: the water's own preference for flow. There. The west pilings create a channel where the current accelerates, and more importantly, where the Warden's chains overhead leave a blind angle, a route hidden in plain sight.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: What's Vess asking you to do, Petra?

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm notices Petra's departure and makes a quiet excuse to the sergeant—something about checking the mooring-chains or the water level. He slips away from the lantern-light into the darkness and descends the rickety ladder carefully, hand on the wet wood, picking his way between the stilts toward the sound of bailing and Vess's muttered curses. When he reaches the water's edge, he surveys the half-swamped punt and its cargo of debts, his eyes moving between the ferryman and his companion.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I've patched wounds that wouldn't stop bleeding and brought babies into storms—this boat's nothing but broken wood and panic. We'll have it seaworthy before those Wardens even realize we're gone.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock descends the ladder without hesitation and wades into the black water beside Vess. She examines the hull with practiced hands, her fingers finding the worst leaks and weak seams. She commandeers tools without asking and sets to work, moving with the same grim efficiency she brings to deliveries in impossible conditions.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: They're split thin and scared—that sergeant's whole attention is turned inland, worrying about what's creeping into town, not watching what leaves. The rain's drowning their sound discipline. We'll have a window if we move when Rell shifts his eyes inland again.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow climbs down to join them under the platform, moving into the shadows between the stilts where he can watch both the dark water below and the torchlight filtering through the planks above. He traces the Wardens' patrol patterns, reading the gaps in their coverage the way he reads water-flow.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Between the four of you the punt goes from wreck to worthy in near silence. Caddock's hands find every weak seam and pack them tight before the leaks can spread, while overhead Yarrow tracks Rell's every restless turn — the sergeant's eyes stay fixed inland, chasing shadows that aren't there, and never once dip toward the water. Petra's read on the current proves true: the west pilings hide a blind channel right under the chains, fast-flowing and drowned in the rain's noise. Vess stares at the sealed hull, then at the clear black water, like a man who hasn't been this close to a clean escape in years. "That's... that's it, then," he breathes, bailing pot forgotten in his hand. He owes Petra now, properly, and he knows it — and so does she. Before dawn breaks and the toll-gate wakes fully to its business, the punt slides free between the pilings, past the Wardens' blind angle, and out into open water, nobody the wiser.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Mireth sold out a girl showing the first marks of hive-touch—her skin rippling, her eyes not quite focused. I'd come to her inn trying to learn if there was any soul left beneath the infection, if the hive could even be reasoned with. When the Wardens came sniffing around, Mireth gave her up rather than lose her license. I promised Mireth that I wouldn't hold it against her, that I understood what hunger and fear make us do. I meant it then. I mean it now.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I see you in there, Mireth. I remember what I promised you. Go—save yourself. The rest of you, move.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm accepts the compel on 'A Weary Innkeeper'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: A weary innkeeper Anselm once trusted for dry shelter — a woman named Mireth, who kept a lean-to near the old mill road — has sold out her latest lodgers, a hollow-eyed hive-touched family she hid for coin, straight to the pack hunting them. They come howling out of the reeds at Gullet Ford, following her betrayal like a scent. attacks at Gullet Ford using hooked spears thrust from the reed banks, because A long groan rises up through the waterlogged stone beneath the ford, the old shrine warning it's about to fall, and the tremor shudders through the mud and drives the hive-touched out of their collapsing den, starving and desperate for the first warm bodies they find..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The punt scrapes gravel at Gullet Ford just as a groan rolls up through the waterlogged stone underfoot — the old shrine beneath the crossing shifting, cracking, warning everyone within earshot that it means to fall. Then the reeds erupt: hollow-eyed shapes, the same hive-touched family Mireth traded away for a dry license, burst from their collapsing den with hooked spears wrenched from broken fence-stakes, pain-blind and starving, driven straight at the first warm bodies they find. Anselm's promise to Mireth curdles in his mouth — he understands now exactly what her fear cost these people. Water churns black around the punt's hull as the family closes from both banks, and somewhere beneath the mud the shrine groans again, closer to giving way.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The shrine's singing—I hear it in the water, in the stone, like Saint Orrin's bells tolling backward. The north anchor-stones still hold, but the southern face is fractured. That's where it fails first.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's eyes go distant as her ears catch the rising wail beneath the churning water. This is the sound she knows from years of bell-work: stone at the breaking point. She traces the shrine's death-song through the groaning beneath the ford, reading the fractures like a bell-pattern, and shouts the safe path to her companions—pulling them toward the ground that will still hold when the ancient stones give way.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I know these waters, I know these stones—I've swum over them since I was small enough to drown. The shrine falls east. There's a channel there. Go. Now.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm closes his eyes for a heartbeat, listening past the rain and spear-clang to the ancient stone groaning beneath the ford. He's swum these broken mill-roads all his life, felt how they collapse. When he opens his eyes, he points sharply toward the eastern bank where the shrine's voice cracks most ominously—recognizing in that sound the exact pattern of collapse, the direction the stone will fall, the channel that will open.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Hold fast. I've faced worse than starving things in the dark.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock seizes the punt pole and steps forward with unshakeable calm, her body positioned between the attacking pack and her companions, ready to meet their hooked spears with solid wood and steady hands.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: North flank is stable—move through there now!

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Brack's warning cuts through the rain as the family bursts from the reeds with their hooked spears. Yarrow's eyes snap across the ford, reading water and ground like he reads every weathered waterway—marking which stones of the old shrine still hold true beneath the floodwater, where solid ground remains clear for the retreat.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I hear my sister in that cry, but she's not here. These people are. I won't hesitate now.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm refuses a compel.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The shrine gives its last warning groan and starts to go — but by then it doesn't matter. Petra's reading of the death-song, Anselm's memory of these drowned mill-roads, and Yarrow's eye for the one strip of stone still holding true all point the same way, and the punt threads through the collapse like it was never in danger at all: north flank solid, east channel open, the party moving as one while the ford buckles behind them. Caddock plants herself between the reeds and her companions and meets the hive-touched family's rush with the pole itself, driving one attacker back bloodied and reeling — Mireth's betrayal has cost these people enough, and Caddock's steady hands make sure it doesn't cost them their lives too, though a hooked spear rakes her ribs before the pack breaks off, scattering into the reeds as the last archway of the shrine slumps into the water behind them. Anselm doesn't get the reckoning he came for — no words with the girl, no proof the hive leaves anything human behind — but he doesn't hesitate either, and that refusal costs him nothing but the ghost of his sister's voice, unanswered, in the rain. The punt scrapes clear onto solid ground on the far bank, soaked, shaken, gear intact, the shrine's grave sealed by broken stone.
